lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4's big question, what could you do when you heard a better reason? (Change your mind.) Today's big question: what do we owe each other? Think, give reasons, and build on others' ideas.

Do we owe anything to people we do not know? To family, friends and neighbours, to people far away, to animals, or to people not yet born? A duty is something you should do because it is right, even if nobody makes you.
Use thinking words: 'I think… because…', 'I agree with Zara, and I would add…', 'I see it differently, because…' and 'What if…?' Building on someone's idea shows you listened first.

messages: I think we owe everyone help, because...
I agree with Zara, and I would add...
What if someone far away needs help?

lesson.text: Mimi finds a lost bag with a name and 20 gold inside. Nobody saw. Does she owe it to the owner to give it back? What if the owner is rich? What if she needs the gold? Many people say honesty is owed to everyone.

picture.claim: Mimi should give the bag back.

lesson.text: Some say we owe most to the people close to us; others say every person matters equally. Many say both: we care most for those near us, but we still owe everyone fairness, honesty and help in an emergency.
What about people not yet born? If we use up resources or spoil the planet, they will pay the price. Many people think we owe the future a world as good as the one we were given.

Thinkers have argued about questions like these for over 2,000 years, since Socrates in Athens. You may not agree with each other, and that is fine. Listen, give reasons, ask questions, and let good reasons change your mind.

Try it in the world: with friends, list five things everyone in your shared world owes each other, like honesty and help. Agree them with reasons, and put them on a sign. Next year: how a country is run, and human rights.

exercises.hint: Nobody has to make you do it.
choices: something you should do because it is right
exercises.explain: A duty is something you should do because it is right.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence builds on someone's idea?
exercises.hint: Which one shows the speaker listened?
choices: 'I agree with Zara, and I would add…'
exercises.explain: 'I agree with Zara, and I would add…' takes her idea further.

exercises.prompt: In a good discussion, you give reasons for your ideas.
exercises.explain: True: 'I think… because…' gives a reason others can weigh.

exercises.prompt: Who asked big questions in Athens over 2,000 years ago?
exercises.explain: Socrates, a thinker in Athens, asked questions to test ideas.

exercises.prompt: Changing your mind after hearing a better reason is a weakness.
exercises.hint: What do good thinkers do with good reasons?
exercises.explain: False: letting good reasons change your mind is a strength.

exercises.prompt: Mimi finds a bag with a name and 20 gold inside. What is the honest thing to do?
choices: give it back to the owner
exercises.explain: Give it back to the owner: the gold is theirs, even if nobody saw.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: helpful or unhelpful in a discussion?
exercises.explain: Helpful: listening, asking 'What if…?', giving reasons. Unhelpful: interrupting, laughing at ideas.

exercises.prompt: What do many people think we owe people not yet born?
exercises.hint: Who will live on the planet after us?
choices: a world as good as the one we got
exercises.explain: Many think we owe the future a world as good as the one we were given.

exercises.prompt: Match each thinking move to a sentence starter.
matches: I agree, and I would add…
exercises.hint: Listen for the clue word in each starter.
exercises.explain: Agreeing: 'I agree, and I would add…'. Disagreeing: 'I see it differently…'. Wondering: 'What if…?'. A reason: 'because'.

exercises.prompt: People can disagree about big questions and both give good reasons.
exercises.hint: Is there always one right answer to a big question?
exercises.explain: True: big questions often have more than one reasonable answer.

exercises.prompt: In many people's view, what do we owe everyone, even strangers?
exercises.hint: Think of what you would want from a stranger.
choices: fairness, honesty and help in an emergency
exercises.explain: Many say everyone is owed fairness, honesty and help in an emergency.

exercises.prompt: Zara says: 'We only owe things to our friends.' Which reply builds on her idea politely?
exercises.hint: Show you listened, then add a question.
choices: I see why, but what about strangers in danger?
exercises.explain: 'I see why, but what about strangers in danger?' respects her idea and adds a new thought.

exercises.prompt: Why might we owe care to animals?
exercises.hint: What do animals and people share?
choices: they can feel pain and fear
exercises.explain: Many animals can feel pain and fear, so many people think we owe them care.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a good discussion in order.
exercises.hint: You cannot build on ideas you have not heard.
items: build on or change your view
give your view with a reason
exercises.explain: Listen, give your view with a reason, listen to others, then build on or change your view.

exercises.prompt: A duty is only something the law makes you do.
exercises.hint: Does any law make you say thank you?
exercises.explain: False: a duty is something you should do because it is right, law or no law.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentence starters by thinking move.
items: I agree, and I would add…
exercises.hint: Does it add to an idea, push back on it, or open a new question?
exercises.explain: Agreeing: 'I agree, and I would add…', 'Yes, and also…'. Disagreeing: 'I see it differently…', 'I think the opposite…'. Wondering: 'What if…?', 'I wonder whether…'.

exercises.prompt: Match each one to something many people say we owe them.
items: the owner of a lost bag
matches: a world as good as ours
exercises.hint: Cards 3, 4 and 5 give an idea for each one.
exercises.explain: Strangers in danger: help in an emergency. People not yet born: a world as good as ours. Animals: care, because they can feel pain. The owner of a lost bag: honesty, so give it back.

exercises.prompt: Sort the reasons: about the people close to us, or about everyone?
items: I care for my family most.
Neighbours look out for each other.
exercises.hint: Does the reason talk about family, friends and neighbours, or about every person?
exercises.explain: Close to us: caring for family most, friends helping friends, neighbours looking out for each other. Everyone: every person matters equally, honesty is owed to all. Many people hold both views at once.
